item.title: Effects of dance and music training on the plasticity of the core empathy network: intra- and inter-network connectivity.
item.description:
PeerJ
Background Dance and music are two of the oldest and most universal forms of artistic expression, each requiring extensive training. Prolonged training is known to induce neuroplastic changes and enhance socio-emotional abilities such as empathy. The mirror neuron system (MNS) is associated with empathy; however, few studies systematically explored how dance and music training modulate the core empathy network, including subcortical regions within the limbic MNS. Method Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data were obtained from 25 dancers, 24 musicians and 39 demographically matched control group (both groups are healthy). Core regions within relevant brain networks, along with key subcortical components of limbic MNS, specifically the amygdala and basal ganglia, were defined as regions of interest (ROIs) to build a core empathy network. Graph-theoretical metrics, including within-network degree (WND) and between-network degree (BND), were calculated to evaluate connectivity patterns. These metrics were further correlated with empathy scores. Results Both dancers and musicians exhibited altered connectivity within the core empathy network. Dancers showed increased WND and BND between basal ganglia regions and the ventral attention network, whereas musicians demonstrated enhanced WND between the amygdala and the subcortical network. Notably, both groups exhibited reduced WND between the superior frontal gyrus and the sensorimotor network. The neural changes were correlated with Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI) empathy subscale scores, indicating training-related modulations in affective and cognitive empathy. Conclusion Dance and music training induce both distinct and overlapping patterns of neuroplasticity within the core empathy network that are associated with enhanced empathic ability. The findings support the potential of dance and music as systematic intervention programs.

item.title: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension—using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation—is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince , in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

item.title: Development of Neonatal Functional Brain Network Organisation and Its Association with Childhood Neurodevelopmental Outcomes
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The human brain undergoes rapid dynamic changes in the neonatal period that are essential for later cognitive and behavioural performance. Using resting-state fMRI data from 394 neonates (325 term-born, 69 preterm-born) within the first month after birth, we characterised the early development of functional network organisation, the effects of preterm birth, and the association between neonatal functional organisation and later neurodevelopmental outcomes in infancy (18 months) and childhood (4-6 years). We found increased functional integration and segregation across a wide range of functional sub-networks and increased mean functional connectivity strength (mean FCS) within the subcortical and cerebellar regions with increasing PMA at scan. Compared with term-born neonates, preterm-born neonates showed significantly lower mean FCS, functional integration and segregation globally. We further showed that whilst neonatal functional brain network organisation was not associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes measured during infancy (18 months), it was associated with later neurodevelopmental outcomes in early childhood (4-6 years). Specifically, higher functional integration and segregation at birth were linked with lower SDQ total difficulties score at 4-6 years. Our findings suggest that neonatal functional brain organisation reflects not only transient developmental processes, but also stable individual differences that provide insight into neurodevelopmental outcomes in later childhood.

item.title: Faster peak alpha frequency precedes higher menstrual pain in adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Brain differences in chronic pain are almost always measured after years of pain experience, leaving unresolved whether they create vulnerability to pain or result from it. Uniquely, menstrual pain has a developmentally scheduled onset (menarche, the first menstrual period), allowing the brain to be characterized before and after pain exposure occurs. Here we used longitudinal 64-channel EEG to measure resting brain activity in adolescents once before (n=250) and twice after (n=161, n=140) menarche. Before their first period, adolescents who later reported higher menstrual pain (30 or greater on a 0 to 100 VAS) already showed faster occipital peak alpha frequency compared to those who reported lower menstrual pain, a difference that persisted in the early (3 to 14 months) post-menarche time period. In contrast, oscillatory power and functional connectivity did not differ by menstrual pain group, suggesting that the widespread functional brain alterations reported in adults with painful periods take years to emerge. Peak alpha frequency increased, and theta power and connectivity decreased across the menarchal transition, consistent with typical adolescent maturation. However, longitudinal analyses stratified by higher and lower menstrual pain group suggested group specific timings for these neurodevelopmental changes. Overall, these findings suggest that early menstrual pain is not associated with widespread alterations in neural oscillations, but aspects of menstrual pain susceptibility may be reflected in resting peak alpha frequency. To our knowledge, this is the first neurophysiological trait shown to precede the onset of menstrual pain.

item.title: Frequency-Specific Cognitive Control Network Hypoconnectivity in Adolescents With Elevated Externalizing Symptoms
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Externalizing symptoms during adolescence are associated with behavioral difficulties and an increased risk of adverse developmental outcomes, and are often accompanied by difficulties in self-regulation across cognitive and emotional domains. Although prior neuroimaging studies have reported altered brain connectivity in externalizing psychopathology, most evidence comes from functional magnetic resonance imaging, leaving frequency-specific electrophysiological network dynamics poorly understood. We examined resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) functional connectivity in a community-based sample of 35 adolescents aged 13–15 years with relatively high or low parent-reported externalizing symptoms. Source-level connectivity was estimated using exact low-resolution electromagnetic tomography and lagged phase synchronization across delta-to-gamma frequency bands within the cognitive control network (CCN) and default mode network (DMN). Results Adolescents with higher externalizing symptoms showed reduced connectivity in five beta1- and gamma-band CCN connections, whereas no significant group differences were observed within the DMN. After adjustment for internalizing symptoms, bilateral anterior-insula connectivity in the beta1 band and left anterior insula–right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex connectivity in the gamma band remained significant. Lower left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex–right inferior frontal junction beta1 connectivity was also associated with greater self-reported physical aggression. Conclusions Elevated externalizing symptoms during adolescence may be linked to altered functional coordination within the cognitive control network. These findings highlight the potential value of frequency-resolved EEG connectivity for characterizing the neural correlates of adolescent externalizing symptoms.

item.title: Interactions between age and sex in multiscale entropy and spectral power changes across the lifespan.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Multiscale entropy (MSE) changes in relation to age, whereby ageing is associated with an increasing bias towards fine scale entropy. This change is thought to represent a shift towards localized information processing in the brain as we age. However, this relationship has not been tested in large sample sizes alongside other demographic factors and cognitive behaviours. This study aimed to replicate previously reported effects of ageing on MSE in an open access database (Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience, N = 587) and expand the findings to include an investigation of the effects of sex and a variety of cognitive behaviours. MSE curves and power spectrum densities (PSD) were calculated for each region of interest from the magnetoencephalography data. Multivariate partial least squares analyses were used to assess the relationship between MSE or PSD and five behavioural/demographic factors including age, sex, fluid intelligence, visual short-term memory, and a generalized measure of cognitive function. Age was associated with increased fine scale and decreased coarse scale entropy, as well as complementary spectral changes, including slowing of peak alpha rhythms, increased beta-band activity, and reduced gamma-band activity, which replicates prior MSE and PSD findings. In both domains, these age-related patterns differentiated based on sex with advancing age. Importantly, the unique effects of sex diverged between MSE and PSD. This result indicates that entropy-based measures can isolate aspects of temporal organization that are not clearly summarized by spectral structure alone.

item.title: Beta-band dynamics during a naturalistic motor task: An OPM-MEG study.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Beta oscillations are a fundamental feature of brain activity, linked to long-range connectivity within canonical networks, inhibition of sensorimotor cortices, and the maintenance of a stable sensorimotor state in situations where the external world is predictable. The importance of beta oscillations in brain function is underscored by observations of their perturbation in neurological and psychiatric disorders. However, the precise role played by beta activity, particularly in mediating complex or skilful movements, remains incompletely understood. Here, we used a newly developed wearable optically pumped magnetometer-based magnetoencephalography (OPM-MEG) system to measure beta dynamics as participants learned to play a musical instrument. Twenty-two novice players took part in a study in which OPM-MEG data were recorded during two scanning sessions, while participants attempted to play a tune on a violin. Between the two sessions, participants received a violin lesson from an expert teacher. Results showed that robust data could be acquired during this naturalistic task, with beta oscillations decreasing in amplitude during movement and increasing upon movement cessation, as expected. Moreover, beta power while playing, in the motor and pre-motor areas, was significantly elevated after the lesson compared to before, and the movement-related modulation of beta amplitude was more pronounced after the lesson. These findings align with predictive coding models which suggest that beta amplitude should increase when individuals have greater certainty over the movements they carry out. Our study adds to an expanding literature on the role of beta oscillations and provides further evidence for the utility of OPM-MEG in naturalistic neuroscience.

item.title: Infra-slow brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions reveal a co-ordinated multisystem physiological network in humans.
item.description:
The Journal of physiology
Growing evidence indicates that brain continuously interacts with other physiological systems through neural and non-neural pathways. The brain-heart and brain-gut axes play a central role in homoeostasis, allostasis and behaviour, but also in cognitive aspects, including emotion and decision-making. Disruptions in these axes have been linked to a wide range of cardiovascular, neurological and psychiatric disorders. Despite this evidence, triadic crosstalk between the brain, heart and gut remains largely unexplored. Brain activity, cardiac autonomic fluctuations and gastric rhythms all exhibit slow temporal components in resting state, suggesting that brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions may occur over time scales from the infra-slow (0.01-0.1 Hz) physiological range. Using open-access electrophysiological recordings from 28 healthy subjects at rest, we extracted time-varying power dynamics describing the activity of the three organs: brain alpha power, cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic indices, and the power of the gastric rhythm. Statistical associations among these organs were quantified using the maximal information coefficient across the extended temporal delay range. Physiological interactions were confirmed using surrogate-based testing, which allowed us to construct the network topology of interactions between the three organs. Our findings show that triadic brain-heart-gut interactions form a multidirectional network primarily at infra-slow time scales during resting state. This study offers one of the first insights into the physiology of brain-heart-gut interplay, providing a methodological baseline for the development of more comprehensive biomarkers based on network dynamics capable of linking pathological conditions to dysregulation across multiple organ systems. KEY POINTS: First in-human, non-invasive investigation of parallel brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions in awake, healthy subjects. We analysed simultaneous electroencephalographic (EEG), electrocardiographic (ECG) and electrogastrographic (EGG) recordings and quantified strength and temporal scale of the derived time series associations to construct a large-scale network of interactions. We found that brain-heart-gut interactions extend into the infra-slow range (0.01-0.1 Hz), indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in the electrophysiological activity of one organ at rest are typically followed by corresponding changes in the other two. We consistently found a robust brain-heart-gut network topology across subjects, with multidirectional interactions and bodily dynamics converging towards midline central-posterior EEG regions. These findings provide one of the first endeavours in characterizing the physiology of brain-heart-gut interactions and a methodology with strong biomarker development potential.

item.title: Gamma-band network segregation links corollary discharge dysfunction and anomalous self-experiences in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Schizophrenia research
Anomalous self-experiences (ASEs) are a core feature of psychotic disorders and reflect disturbances in ipseity. Impairments in corollary discharge mechanism have been proposed as a neurobiological substrate of ASEs, and an imbalance between brain network integration and segregation, may impair the coherent flow of mental contents, thereby disrupting their fluid and implicit character. However, the relationship between corollary discharge and functional network properties has not been directly examined. This link was assessed in thirty participants with schizophrenia and thirty healthy controls. Functional network was computed using the Phase Locking Value (PLV) from resting-state EEG in the gamma band and two parameters were calculated: the clustering coefficient (ClC, as a proxy for segregation) and the path length (PL, as a proxy for integration); corollary discharge was indexed by N1 suppression in a talk-listen paradigm; and ASEs were evaluated using the 'Inventory of Psychotic-Like Anomalous Self-Experiences' (IPASE) total score. Patients with schizophrenia showed significantly greater gamma-band network segregation and lower integration than healthy controls. Moreover, higher segregation in this band was associated with reduced N1 suppression and greater ASEs severity in patients, whereas network integration was not associated with N1 suppression nor ASEs. These findings suggest that excessive gamma-band network segregation may be correlated with disrupted corollary discharge functioning and may compromise the distinction between self-generated and external stimuli. Therefore, it may alter the sense of ipseity by interfering with the integration of mental contents into the flow of consciousness, thereby contributing to greater severity of ASEs.

item.title: Reduced short-lag autoregressive carry-over in resting-state latent dynamics in major depressive disorder.
item.description:
Psychiatry research. Neuroimaging
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is increasingly characterized as a disorder of brain dynamics, but the temporal scale on which resting-state activity differs from healthy controls remains unclear. We analyzed resting-state fMRI data from 71 participants (51 MDD, 20 controls; OpenNeuro ds002748) using bilateral grid-extracted left-right difference signals projected into a control-defined latent space. Across 30 analysis configurations spanning five denoising pipelines, three latent dimensionalities, and two left-right correction settings, MDD showed reduced mean lag-1 autocorrelation in 24 of 30 configurations (integrated β = -0.0321, p = 0.036) and reduced AR(1) gain φ in 24 of 30 (β = -0.0316, p = 0.037), both robust to adjustment for pipeline, age, sex, and head motion. The broader autocorrelation area under lags 1-10 was not significantly reduced (β = -0.0099, p = 0.22), and lag-by-lag analysis localized the group difference specifically to lag 1. A model-comparison analysis identified AR-gain reduction as one of three competing candidate generative transformations rather than the unique winner. MDD is thus associated with a focal short-lag autoregressive carry-over reduction, a candidate latent-dynamical phenotype rather than a fully identified mechanism.

item.title: Left Temporoparietal Neural Synchrony Tracks Cooperative Performance Across Adult Dyads
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cooperation requires interacting individuals to coordinate their actions toward shared goals, and interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) has been proposed as a neural correlate of this coordination. However, the relationship between INS and cooperative performance remains heterogeneous, and relatively little is known about how it varies across social relationships. The present study examined INS and behavioral performance during a naturalistic cooperative tabletop Jenga task in close-friend, romantic-partner, and mother–child dyads (N = 284 participants). Brain activity was simultaneously recorded using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning, and INS was quantified using wavelet transform coherence across the bilateral inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and temporoparietal junction (TPJ). Cooperative performance was assessed using tower collapse and the number of valid turns completed during the game. True interacting dyads exhibited significantly greater neural synchrony than surrogate dyads across all examined regional pairings ( d range = 0.35–0.55), indicating robust interaction-related inter-brain synchrony. Behavioral performance was not associated with INS at the whole-network level. Region-specific analyses, however, showed that tower collapse was associated with reduced synchrony in the left TPJ–left TPJ ( p Bonf = 0.009) and left TPJ–right TPJ ( p Bonf = 0.017) pairings, whereas the number of valid turns was unrelated to INS. Follow-up analyses further indicated that the association between tower collapse and left TPJ–left TPJ synchrony was present in close-friend ( p Bonf = 0.020) and romantic-partner ( p Bonf = 0.026) dyads but not in mother–child dyads. These findings suggest that the behavioral relevance of interpersonal neural synchrony is not uniform, but depends on the neural systems involved, the specific index of cooperative performance, and the relational and developmental context in which interaction unfolds.

item.title: Accentuated Divergence, Constrained Expression: Autistic Traits Modulate the Creative Brain in Adults with ADHD
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition, and co-occurring autistic traits may shape its phenotypic expression. Although creativity has been discussed as a relative strength in ADHD, it remains unclear whether autistic traits are associated with different dimensions of creativity in adults with ADHD and whether large-scale brain networks contribute to these associations. Methods We compared divergent thinking (DT) and real-life creativity between 65 adults with ADHD and 73 neurotypical controls. We used subgroup comparisons, partial correlation analyses, and multiple regression models to determine the effects of autistic traits (ATs) on creativity dimensions within the ADHD cohort. Guided by prior creativity-network research, we analyzed resting-state functional connectivity (FC) of the Default Mode Network (DMN) and Frontoparietal Network (FPN) to uncover the neural mechanisms. Results The ADHD cohort demonstrated significantly higher scores on both DT ( p s = 0.002–0.009) and real-life creativity measures ( p s = 0.011–0.017) compared to the neurotypical control group. Importantly, increased ATs within the ADHD group were associated with a dissociated creativity profile, showing positive associations with DT but negative associations with real-life creativity. At the neural level, stronger right DMN–FPN connectivity mediated positive associations between ATs and DT performance (ps = 0.007–0.018), but mediated a negative association between ATs and self-reported imagination (p = 0.029). Conclusions In individuals with ADHD, co-occurring ATs exert a paradoxical effect on creativity, enhancing DT while compromising real-life creative achievement. In this subgroup with ADHD and elevated ATs, interventions should capitalize on ATs-associated ideational strengths while circumventing translational barriers, to enhance real-world creative outcomes.

item.title: Auditory Stimulation-Evoked Frontoparietal Theta Asymmetry for Subtype Classification and Long-Term Prognosis Prediction in Disorders of Consciousness.
item.description:
Brain sciences
Background : Quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG) facilitates the objective assessment of residual brain function in patients with disorders of consciousness (DOC), which addresses the intrinsic limitations of behavioral assessment methods. Nevertheless, the characteristics of frontoparietal neural oscillation asymmetry between resting state and auditory stimulation state have not been fully elucidated, and its incremental prognostic value for DOC subtype classification and outcome prediction remains to be confirmed. Methods : Fifty-seven patients with DOC and 23 healthy controls completed qEEG recordings at baseline and during auditory stimulation. Interhemispheric asymmetry indices of the frontal lobe and parietal lobe were calculated for the theta band and alpha band. Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) were adopted to test the main effects and interaction effects of diagnosis, brain region and stimulation condition. The correlations between asymmetry indicators, Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) scores and 6-month Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) scores were analyzed. Nested logistic regression and Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis were performed to quantify the incremental prognostic value of oscillatory asymmetry beyond conventional clinical variables; odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for all predictive indicators. Internal leave-one-out cross-validation and external cohort validation were performed to assess the generalizability and robustness of the final prognostic model. Results : Significant diagnosis × region interaction effects were observed in both frequency bands. Vegetative state (VS) patients presented with frontal-dominant asymmetry, while minimally conscious state (MCS) patients showed parietal-dominant asymmetry; this dissociative pattern was significantly amplified after auditory stimulation. Only stimulation-evoked theta asymmetry showed consistent correlations with clinical status and prognosis: frontal theta asymmetry was negatively correlated with CRS-R scores, while parietal theta asymmetry was positively correlated with CRS-R scores and 6-month GOS outcomes. Incorporating stimulated frontoparietal theta asymmetry significantly improved prognostic performance, and the area under the curve (AUC) of the optimal model reached 0.930. Conclusions : VS and MCS present distinct frontoparietal oscillatory asymmetry phenotypes, which are specifically enhanced by auditory stimulation. Stimulation-evoked theta band asymmetry can reflect residual conscious function and provides incremental prognostic value for long-term functional recovery, with robust generalizability verified by internal and external validation.

item.title: Predicting upcoming visual features during eye movements yields scene representations aligned with human visual cortex.
item.description:
Science advances
Natural scenes are complex arrangements of objects, surfaces, and backgrounds. For the brain's visual system to effectively operate, it needs to extract not only what objects are present but also their spatial and semantic relations. We hypothesize that such structures may be learned, in a self-supervised fashion, by exploiting temporal regularities of natural active vision: Each fixation reveals a glimpse that is related to the previous one via co-occurrence and saccade-conditioned spatial regularities. We instantiate this idea with glimpse prediction networks (GPNs), recurrent models trained to predict the embedding of the next glimpse along human-like scanpaths. GPNs are shown to successfully extract complex scene information, including object co-occurrences and spatial object arrangements, and integrate information across glimpses. GPN representations align strongly with human fMRI responses in mid- and higher-level visual cortex and match, often outperform, alternative state-of-the-art ANN models, establishing next-glimpse-prediction as a biologically plausible route toward brain-aligned scene representations.

item.title: EEG Edge-Centric Dynamics Reveal Distinct Post-Stroke Somatosensory Network Responses to Vibratory and Electrical Stimulation.
item.description:
IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics
Stroke-induced somatosensory deficits disrupt sensorimotor integration (SMI) and limit motor recovery, yet the immediate network-level effects of different somatosensory interventions remain unclear, hindering patient-specific rehabilitation planning. We propose an informatics framework based on edge-centric dynamic connectivity (ECDC) to characterize transient, whole-brain EEG network responses to sensory-level focal vibratory stimulation (FVS) and neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES). We analyzed EEG recordings from 15 chronic stroke participants and 15 healthy controls during forearm stimulation and quantified temporal network dynamics, spectral network organization, and interhemispheric interactions from instantaneous overlapping functional networks. Compared with NMES, FVS in stroke participants induced a distinct neurophysiological profile, including (i) shorter global theta-network latency, suggesting faster attentional engagement; (ii) higher contralesional alpha network diversity, indicating enhanced somatosensory recruitment; and (iii) reduced theta-alpha phase-amplitude coupling, reflecting decoupled interhemispheric interactions that may support adaptive reorganization. These findings provide interpretable network signatures for differentiating stimulation-specific brain responses and suggest a data driven route toward personalized SMI rehabilitation.

item.title: Naturalistic spatial education engages distinct neural processes for mental rotation, cognitive load, and linguistic demands.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Neuroscience studies typically isolate spatial cognition using simplified tasks targeting a single cognitive process. However, during formal spatial education, the brain rarely performs one cognitive operation at a time. Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess neural systems involved in dynamically processing an educational spatial visualization lesson. We quantified lesson content using an instructional-design framework capturing variation in spatial complexity, cognitive load, and verbal density. We then characterized how instructional demands modulated brain function using content-evoked responses, functional connectivity, and network-centrality. Spatial transformations during instruction robustly recruited parietal and premotor regions, which were linearly modulated by spatial complexity. This parietal dominance aligns with theories that these areas encode geometric and quantitative dimensions. In contrast, domain-general frontal activity tracked overall processing demands, and language regions tracked verbal density. Activity also varied with learners' spatial abilities: higher spatial performers showed stronger modulation of parietal and premotor regions as spatial demands increased, and greater domain-general modulation across content types. Thus, the same circuitry representing spatial transformations during instruction also reflects individual variation in spatial cognition. Parietal regions showed the highest centrality and strongest within-network coherence, marking them as the central hub of the system, and distinguishing them from less central and less coherent domain-general regions. Together, the findings reveal how the brain dynamically decomposes complex spatial instruction, preserving parietal-centered spatial processing, while coordinating support from premotor, domain-general, and language systems. These findings begin to reveal how spatial cognition operates within the complexity of formal instruction.

item.title: Thalamocortical dysconnectivity shapes cortical hierarchy disruption across illness durations in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Background Schizophrenia is increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of circuit-level dysfunction. However, how thalamocortical abnormalities differ across cohorts with varying illness durations and relate to large-scale cortical hierarchical organization remains unclear. Methods We analyzed resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 1,223 patients with schizophrenia and 1,224 matched healthy controls across 12 datasets. The datasets were grouped as early-, middle-, and late-stage cohorts. Connectivity gradient mapping was applied to characterize thalamocortical organization, and computational modeling evaluated simulated hierarchical changes after modifying thalamic-salience connectivity. Results We identified a schizophrenia-relevant sensorimotor-salience-association axis that captures systematic differences in thalamocortical abnormality profiles across the stage cohorts. Along this axis, case-control effects in association regions were positive in the early-stage cohort but negative in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, whereas sensorimotor regions showed the converse pattern. This cross-cohort pattern was accompanied by reduced cortical hierarchical separation in cohorts with longer illness duration. In contrast, salience-related thalamic regions showed negative case-control effects in all three stage cohorts, with larger effect sizes in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, and these alterations were associated with clinical symptoms. Computational modification of thalamic-salience connectivity increased simulated cortical hierarchical differentiation, particularly in the middle-stage cohort. Conclusions These findings indicate that thalamocortical dysconnectivity, centered on disrupted thalamic-salience interactions, is associated with systematic differences in cortical hierarchical organization across cohorts. The cross-cohort pattern of salience-related abnormalities highlights thalamic-salience coupling as a circuit-level link to cortical hierarchical differentiation and a candidate for future mechanistic and interventional investigation.

item.title: REM Sleep Iota Oscillations Across the Lifespan
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Iota oscillations are a newly discovered marker of wakefulness and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. So far, iota in REM sleep has only been reported in the surface electroencephalography (EEG) of a small sample of young adults and in intracranial recordings of epileptic patients. Here, we investigated the presence of these oscillations in a large dataset (N=937) of high-density sleep EEG recordings from individuals 7 to 70 years old. We found that iota spectral peaks during REM sleep were between 25 and 40 Hz, slightly faster than in wake (25-35 Hz). Iota power was significantly associated with REM sleep architecture, increasing with both REM duration and across progressive sleep cycles. Iota peaks were observed in individuals of all ages, although the prevalence decreased gradually with age, from 88% in children to 44% in older adults. Most iota spectral peak properties (frequency, amplitude, timing, topography) likewise shifted with age. The most striking effect, however, was in bandwidth, such that children had narrow iota peaks, older adults had broad iota peaks, and 20-30 year olds could have either. It remains unclear whether narrowband and broadband iota are functionally equivalent. On shorter time scales (< 1 year), iota properties remained stable across measurements. Analyses of a separate dataset of monozygotic and dizygotic twins revealed high heritability of all iota peak properties except bandwidth. Overall, these results establish iota as a genetically determined trait-like marker of REM sleep with unique age-related changes. Iota oscillations open new avenues to investigate the interaction between sleep, genetics, development, and aging.

item.title: Neurodegeneration epicenters: Distinct network mechanisms of dopaminergic treatment in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Neural regeneration research
Abstract Parkinson's disease exhibits heterogeneous spatiotemporal patterns of neurodegeneration. Dopaminergic therapy improves motor symptoms by modulating brain function in affected regions, yet whether the neural mechanisms through which dopaminergic therapy exerts its effects are linked to this heterogeneity of neurodegeneration remains unclear. A connectivity-based epicenter framework combined with spectral dynamic causal modeling was applied to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 160 drug-naïve Parkinson's disease patients and 174 healthy controls to identify subtype-specific degenerative epicenters and characterize directional interactions among affected regions. Ninety-seven patients additionally underwent an acute levodopa challenge to evaluate how dopaminergic modulation influences these interactions and relates to symptom improvements. Two distinct Parkinson's disease subtypes were identified: subtype 1 was characterized by degenerative epicenters predominantly located in subcortical and cerebellar regions, whereas subtype 2 exhibited epicenters primarily involving cortical regions. Both subtypes exhibited widespread dysregulation of directional interactions among epicenter regions relative to healthy controls. Levodopa treatment partially reversed these network abnormalities in a manner specific to each subtype, notably within cerebellar vermis in subtype 1 and frontal cortex in subtype 2. Symptom improvements were linked to distinct network interactions: in subtype 1, tremor correlated with the thalamus, midbrain nuclei, and cerebellar vermis, whereas bradykinesia primarily involved the cerebellar vermis; in subtype 2, rigidity improvements mapped to frontal cortex and limbic regions, and bradykinesia to limbic regions. These findings suggest that Parkinson's disease involves distinct epicenter networks in each subtype, with widespread directional dysregulation contributing to symptom diversity in patients. Levodopa treatment selectively modulates these network interactions, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying treatment heterogeneity and guiding precision-targeted therapeutic strategies.

item.title: Cerebral Hemodynamic Patterns in People with Subjective Cognitive Decline: A Systematic Review Based on Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy.
item.description:
Brain sciences
Background/Objectives : Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) has been proposed as an early symptomatic manifestation of dementia/Alzheimer's disease. However, its associated brain patterns are not yet fully characterized. In recent years, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has emerged as a cost-effective technique to detect hemodynamic changes associated with cognitive decline. Therefore, fNIRS may be a valuable tool to investigate SCD neural underpinnings. This systematic review synthesizes current fNIRS evidence regarding the hemodynamic correlates of SCD during both resting-state and cognitive task conditions. Methods : Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science databases for studies combining keywords ('subjective cognitive decline', 'cognitive complaints', 'memory complaints', 'fNIRS', and 'near-infrared spectroscopy') with Boolean operators. Results : We identified 181 records, of which 10 studies fulfilled the inclusion and exclusion criteria. All studies were cross-sectional. Furthermore, 33% lacked a healthy control group, 56% lacked a standardized SCD identification protocol, 55% used small or imbalanced samples, and 66% did not clearly differentiate prefrontal subregions. In both resting-state and task conditions, SCD individuals showed heterogeneous hemodynamic responses in prefrontal areas. The severity of SCD and the difficulty of the tasks may be useful moderators of these associations. Conclusions : The limited evidence and methodological differences prevent identifying a specific hemodynamic pattern for SCD. Adopting longitudinal, well-powered, and well-controlled designs will be essential to evaluate fNIRS-derived hemodynamic responses in SCD.

item.title: Functional neuroimaging as a tool to understand social determinants of health in cognitive aging and ADRD: a scoping review
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The social, structural, and physical conditions in which individuals live, work, and age, collectively termed social determinants of health (SDOH), are associated with risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Differences in brain function in later life may offer understanding of how SDOH become biologically embedded and confer differential ADRD risk. However, how functional neuroimaging techniques have been used to study SDOH in cognitive aging and ADRD has yet to be systematically characterized. We therefore conducted a scoping review. Three databases were searched, 2,930 articles were screened, and 41 studies were included. Education was the most frequently studied SDOH domain, accounting for 65.9% (k = 27) of studies, followed by economic and occupation (k = 9, 22.0%), social and community (k = 5, 12.2%), food (k = 4, 9.8%), and physical environment (k = 3, 7.3%). Of the 41 studies, five (12.2%) examined multidomain determinants and one study (2.4%) examined three determinants each from different domains. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was most frequently employed (k = 31, 75.6%), followed by electroencephalography (EEG; k = 7, 17.1%), and magnetoencephalography (MEG; k = 4, 9.8%). One study (2.4%) employed a multimodal approach, while none used functional near-infrared spectroscopy. Resting state paradigms (k = 27, 65.9%) outnumbered task-based (k = 14, 34.1%) and most studies were cross-sectional (k = 38, 92.7%). The predominant focus on education, fMRI, and cross-sectional designs highlights many opportunities for future investigation of how SDOH may be associated with later life brain function.

item.title: Problematic social media and gaming use, screen time, and youth mental health and brain structure in the ABCD Study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
In an increasingly digital age, knowing which kinds of screen use relate to mental health in adolescents could help guide prevention efforts for a vulnerable population. Earlier work has examined this question, but the findings have been difficult to interpret. For instance, most studies measure screen use in hours, while it may be more informative to know whether adolescents have difficulty controlling their use. This is especially important now that adolescents use screens for school, games and contact with friends. Whether these patterns are reflected in the brain also remains largely unexplored. ABCD Study release 7.0 (N=11,860) is well suited to these questions because of its comprehensive profiling across neuroimaging, behavioral and clinical domains. In a preregistered study, we examined how screen time, problematic social media use (SMAQ) and problematic video game use (VGAQ) relate to parent-rated mental health, brain structure and resting-state connectivity. All five confirmatory associations were positive but small (β = 0.051 to 0.173) and remained consistent across several robustness checks. In the same participants, the problematic use scales were more strongly related to attention problems than hours of use were. The association between screen time and anxiety problems was present in male but not female participants. More screen time was associated with slightly smaller putamen and caudate volumes, while resting-state connectivity did not predict SMAQ. In exploratory analyses, SMAQ predicted later attention problems more than the reverse, while for gaming, attention problems predicted later VGAQ more strongly. Most of the association seemed to come from problematic use rather than use time by itself. Overall, the effects were small but consistent, in line with earlier work in the ABCD Study. We hope this analysis can contribute to a better understanding of how social media and gaming relate to adolescent mental health and brain development.

item.title: Personalized Network Mapping Reveals State-Trait Dissociation of Frontoparietal Connectivity in Adolescent Depression: A Longitudinal Study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Prior research linking resting-state networks (RSNs) to adolescent depression has yielded inconsistent findings, partly because group-average templates poorly capture individual brains; a mismatch that may be especially consequential during adolescence, when RSNs grow increasingly heterogeneous across individuals. Using a personalized analysis pipeline in the longitudinal Characterizing Adolescent Trajectories of Depression cohort (38 depressed adolescents [28 female]; ages 14–18; 181 usable scans; avg. participation: 446.18 days), we derived individualized definitions of three canonical depression-related RSNs. Because longitudinal RSN connectivity may reflect both trait-like vulnerability and state-like symptom fluctuation, we used mixed-effects models to decompose connectivity profiles into both components. FPN connectivity showed a significant state-trait dissociation: chronically elevated connectivity predicted greater average symptom burden, while transient increases predicted momentary relief. These effects were undetectable using group-atlas estimates. We suggest FPN connectivity plays a dual, compensatory role in adolescent depression and demonstrate that personalized definitions can reveal clinically meaningful brain–symptom associations.

item.title: Molecularly distinct neurodegeneration shapes the DOPA-dependent dynamic of large-scale brain connectomics in GBA-associated Parkinson’s disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract GBA1-associated Parkinson’s disease (GBA1-PD) is a biologically distinct synucleinopathy associated with glucocerebrosidase deficiency, lysosomal dysfunction, and more extensive cortical neurodegeneration. How these molecular abnormalities shape large-scale cortical network dynamics in vivo remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize resting-state EEG functional connectivity and network topology in GBA1-PD and to determine whether GBA1-related molecular pathology is associated with a distinct oscillatory connectome signature and its modulation by dopaminergic treatment. We recorded resting-state EEG in 22 patients with PD (GBA1-PD = 7; LRRK2-PD = 5; sporadic PD = 10) together with 14 age-matched healthy controls. EEG was acquired in OFF and ON dopaminergic states. Functional connectivity was estimated using imaginary coherence (ImCoh) and phase-locking value (PLV) across canonical frequency bands, while network organization was quantified using the graph-theoretical clustering coefficient. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess therapy- and subtype-specific effects. GBA1-PD exhibited a selective increase in gamma-band clustering coefficient in the ON condition (p = 0.044), which was not observed in LRRK2 or sporadic PD. PLV-based analyses highlighted opposite clustering changes in GBA1 and LRRK2 patients. ImCoh analyses further revealed different therapy-related connectivity changes in genetic and sporadic PD across all frequency bands (all p ≤ 0.0035). Compared with healthy controls, PD was associated with widespread disruption of cortico-cortical connectivity. All significant effects were abolished in surrogate-data analyses, supporting their physiological specificity. Resting-state EEG connectomics may reveal genotype-specific network alterations in GBA1-PD and their modulation by dopaminergic treatment, supporting a relationship between genetic background and large-scale brain network dynamics.
